extracted.intended_audience: learned readers of natural philosophy/occult medicine and practitioners (physicians, magicians, alchemists) in early modern/medieval Europe
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural prescriptions, classifications, and observational rules for producing magical, venefic (poisonous), alchemical, and wondrous effects (e.g., making poisons, inscribing figures on skin, artificial fruits, spontaneous generation experiments) drawn from an early-modern treatise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opium/mandrake-based soporific pomum (sleep-inducing preparation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pomum ex opio & mandragorz succo coa(tum) &o vinifze & zibeto, somnum dulcem & ubertim conciliare potest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agrippa states that a fruit (pomum) treated with opium and mandrake juice, wine and civet (zibeth) produces a sweet and abundant sleep. He notes intended uses (for watching/keeping vigil — e.g., students, the studious, and old men troubled by vigils) and warns that such preparations can be turned to harm or used for illicit ends; the author remarks on both beneficial and malicious uses and cautions about misuse and adulteration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Power of inscribed words on vessels/objects
rubrics_metrics.description: Inscribere verba in vasis/testis/patellis prodire potest: 'Si testas aut patellas tres ... stylo inscribas his verbis... Iao Sabaoth ... in illas congregabitur' (verba valere ad fitendum).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text reports recipes/claims that inscribing specific words on vessels or objects will bring about effects (e.g., gathering of fishes, preservation of wine, miraculous effects involving blood). Examples and author citations are given as evidence; the practice is presented as widespread belief and used as explanation for reported 'miracles'. The passage functions as a procedural claim (inscribe these words to obtain the stated effect) but is presented with varying degrees of scepticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aqua separationis for producing permanent white scars/figures on skin
rubrics_metrics.description: Aqua separetionis (aqua separationis) applied in conjunction with incision and heat can produce an indelible white cicatrix in the form drawn on the skin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure described: depict the desired figure on the skin with black (atramento), incise (novacula), then apply aqua separationis; after heating/contracting the flesh the color consolidates and a perpetual white scar results. The author claims the result is permanent unless intentionally altered, and provides experiential notes (observed effect, need for certain manipulations, use of cantharides to aid ulceration).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of cantharides (spanish fly) as vesicant/exulcerant when combined with separation water
rubrics_metrics.description: Cantharides potentia sunt exulcerantes cutem; aquae separationis imbuta can exulcerare cutem et creare ulcera (used to effect separation/marks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cantharides (blister beetles) are described as able to ulcerate skin; when combined with aqua separationis their potency causes exulceration, useful for producing lasting marks or aiding the skin-separation processes described. Practical note: impregnating the separation water with cantharides makes it act faster and more violently; used where the mark/ulcer is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spider-in-nut poison preservation trick
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment: enclose a spider (aranea) intact between the shell/cortices of a nut (nux inclusa), and if that nut is given in a drink, the poison/effect remains so long as the spider remains confined within the nut's cortices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agrippa relays an experiment (with caution about author credibility): place a whole spider inside a nut between its shells and seal it; this preserved inclusion is claimed to confer poison/effect to any drink given with the nut, and the effect lasts while the spider remains enclosed. Presented as an arcane recipe/apparatus for veneficium; given as a reported practice rather than scientifically explained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Production of a 'stone' (lapis) from putrefied human blood via distillation and calcination
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanguinis humani ... sub equino simo putrefcere ... per vitrum facta destillatione aquam subtrahamus ... calcemus ... vertemus in lapide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stepwise method reported: allow human blood to putrefy for a stated period, perform a distillation (collecting water/spirits), dry and calcine the residues in a glass vessel, and by further heating/calcination convert the material into a red, splendid 'stone' (lapis). Agrippa cites sources (e.g., Agrippa's book on veneficia) and treats this as an alchemical/occult technique; procedural detail and cautions about authorship/credibility are interspersed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of veneficia (poisoning/magic) types
rubrics_metrics.description: Veneficia differuntur: (1) quae sumpta sunt (taken by ingestion), (2) quae ex excrementis corruptis et sanguine vel urina vel partibus animalium conficiuntur (made from corrupt excretions, blood, urine, animal parts), (3) tertium quod 'absque coaréta' fit (a third kind contracted without ingestion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agrippa distinguishes multiple kinds of veneficia and venoms: those administered by eating/drinking; those prepared from corrupt excrements, blood, hair, etc.; and a third type that act without being ingested (via contact, presence, or other means). He notes overlap between veneficia and other magical practices and warns that knowledge of these methods is dangerous and not to be lightly sought—some techniques are morally and physically perilous and often mixed with superstition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sympathetic resonance / transmitted motion via instruments (musical nerve experiment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment with two lyres/strings placed near one another: stretching the first nerve/string and placing the second in supine position produces a similar sound in the second via transmitted motion; 'initrumenta ad igualem sonum' (instruments produce the same sound).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agrippa records a practical demonstration: place two lyres/strings, tune one and touch/stretch nerves so that motion (possibly through the air or sympathetic vibration) causes the adjacent instrument to give the same sound. He conjectures on causes (air moving nerves, equal motion transmitted) and treats it as a 'miraculum' worth attempting. The account is observational and speculative rather than a strict physical theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spontaneous generation via putrefaction (making animals from buried fatty material)
rubrics_metrics.description: Putrefaction of fatty/humid matter buried (often in equine dung or earth) yields generation of worms/animals/serpents; require separation of fat (pingue) from putrescence and burial in certain soils.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author asserts many small animals arise from putrefaction if fatty materials are buried in suitable substrates (e.g., horse dung, certain soils); he gives rules about moisture, separation of fatty matter, and timing, and uses these examples to explain observed 'miracles' of spontaneous generation. He notes variability by region and material and suggests practical cautions: avoid leaving fatty humors exposed if one wishes to prevent such generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of odors, plants and excrements to affect animals and inhibit generation
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain plants and their odors (e.g., ruta) and other materials can repel or attract insects/animals, prevent their breeding, or alter plant/animal properties; likewise, excrements and smells influence local air and generation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agrippa collects many observations: some regions lack certain venomous animals because of climate/food/odors; ruta and other astringent herbs can repel or affect intestinal insects; odors can prevent animals from inhabiting places. He uses these facts to explain why some places breed or lack certain creatures and to instruct about prophylactic/operative measures (e.g., using odors to protect stores or alter generation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Artificial formation of fruits/figures from wood/plants using gypsum and moulding
rubrics_metrics.description: To produce a fruit-shaped object in wood (or to make a wooden mold yield a fruitiform product): carve/prepare a cavity, surround with gypsum (gypso) dissolved in water, possibly coat with oil and dry; repeated packing and care yields an object approximating the desired fruit/form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: form a two-part cavity in wood, fill or coat with gypsum-water mixture and include fragments to imitate pulp; wrap and allow to dry; by careful layering (and choice of plant materials that take form well, e.g., bryony) one can obtain a fruitiform object. Agrippa describes variants, materials to favor (plants that hold form), and cautions about durability and appearance. This is presented as an artisanal/oc cult recipe rather than natural fruit production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ungual (nail) signs as prognostics (nails indicate future events and health)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes in nails (unguis) — color, mutation, and the digit involved — are taken as signs of future events, honors, labors, poverty, calamities or felicities; timing rules are given (e.g., local changes appear earlier and whole-nail changes take longer: 'partem unguis [mutatio] fit septennio, totius ... duodecim').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agrippa reports a system of reading nails: which finger is affected corresponds to a domain (thumb honors/pleasures, index gains, middle finger labors, ring finger dignity, little finger calamities), and the speed/magnitude of change correlates with magnitude/timing of the event. He gives approximate temporal scales (months to years). The material is presented observationally as divinatory practice with many caveats about certainty and variability.
